recipe.history:
Ricotta is one of the oldest and most elemental cheeses in the Italian culinary tradition, its very name — from the Latin recocta, meaning 'recooked' — describing the method by which it is made: fresh whey, the liquid left behind after other cheeses are produced, is heated again until the remaining proteins coagulate into soft, snowy curds. This technique of whey reuse dates back to at least the Bronze Age in Sicily and Sardinia, where pastoral cultures kept large sheep and goat herds and developed an entire economy around transforming animal milk into storable, transportable food. Ancient Greek and Roman texts describe soft white cheeses made from reheated whey; Virgil mentions what appears to be a ricotta-like cheese in the Eclogues. In the medieval period, ricotta appears in the earliest Italian recipe collections — the fourteenth-century Liber de Coquina includes ricotta in pasta dishes and stuffed preparations that bear a clear resemblance to modern lasagna and ravioli. Sicilian and Campanian ricotta, made from the whey of sheep's milk, retains a slightly richer, more complex character than the cow's-milk ricotta that became standard in America; Italian-American immigrants brought their ricotta traditions with them and established the cheese as a cornerstone of Italian-American cooking — in manicotti, stuffed shells, cannoli, and cheesecake.

Ricotta's appearance on a burger represents the Italian-American culinary imagination at its most playful. The cheese's mild, slightly sweet, grainy-creamy texture is the opposite of the sharp, aggressive cheeses most commonly associated with burgers — cheddar, American, blue — and placing it on a beef patty creates a contrast that is immediately surprising and then immediately logical. Ricotta on a burger behaves as both a sauce and a cheese: it spreads, it softens further from the heat of the patty, and it provides a creamy, cooling counterpoint to the seared crust and savory fat of the beef. In restaurants in New York and Los Angeles, ricotta burgers began appearing in the 2010s as chefs with Italian-American roots started rethinking the burger as a canvas for the flavors they grew up with. Fresh herbs, lemon zest, and a drizzle of honey are classic Italian-American accompaniments for ricotta, and they translate to the burger format with immediate success.

I first put ricotta on a burger as a joke — a 'what if' experiment on a Sunday afternoon when I had half a tub of whole-milk ricotta left over from making stuffed shells and a patty that needed to be cooked. I spread the ricotta thick on the bottom bun, added a layer of thinly sliced prosciutto over the warm patty, and finished with fresh basil leaves and a drizzle of honey. I expected to feel silly. Instead I stood at the kitchen counter completely still for a full minute after the first bite, just experiencing the thing I had accidentally made. The ricotta was like a cold, sweet, creamy counterweight to the rich, salty prosciutto and the seared juicy beef. The honey made everything sing. I have never again thought of ricotta as a pasta filling only. It belongs on a burger, and I will defend that position for the rest of my life.

There is no negotiation about medium-rare for a burger that carries ricotta. The cheese is cold and yielding; the contrast with the warm, blushing interior of the patty is one of the great textural pleasures in this burger's construction. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the patty is hot enough to slightly warm the ricotta where they meet, creating a barely perceptible tempering that makes the cheese seem even more luxurious. Cook the patty beyond that range and the beef dries out, its richness replaced by the slightly grainy, slightly livery quality that overcooked ground beef acquires when forced past its ideal temperature. Medium rare is not a suggestion here. It is the condition under which this burger makes sense.
ingredients: 1 tbsp fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil (for dressing arugula)
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Whisk warm milk, sugar, and yeast; rest 5 minutes until foamy. Add butter and egg; mix. Add flour and salt; knead 8–10 minutes until smooth. Rise in an oiled bowl 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 4 balls, flatten slightly, proof on parchment 30–40 minutes. Brush with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 15–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool completely.

2. Prepare the herbed ricotta: In a bowl, combine whole-milk ricotta, chiffonaded basil, parsley, lemon zest, olive oil, salt, pepper, and red pepper flakes. Stir gently until well combined. Taste and adjust seasoning. Refrigerate until ready to assemble — it should be served cold or cool against the warm patty.
3. Dress the arugula: In a small bowl, toss baby arugula with extra-virgin olive oil, lemon juice, and a pinch of flaky salt. Set aside.

4. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Gently combine the garlic powder, dried oregano, salt, and pepper into the beef. Form patties 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, pressing a center dimple. Season outside with additional salt and pepper just before cooking.

5. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until very hot. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Sear patties without moving for 3 minutes. Flip once. Cook 2 more minutes. Target internal temperature: 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest off heat 3 minutes.
6. Toast buns cut-side down in the skillet 60–90 seconds until golden.

7. Assemble: Spread a thick, generous layer of herbed ricotta on the bottom bun — do not be shy; this is the sauce and the cheese in one. Place the medium-rare patty on the ricotta. Lay 2 slices of prosciutto over the patty, folding them loosely so they drape and ruffle. Place a few fresh basil leaves on top of the prosciutto. Add a slice or two of heirloom tomato. Top with a small handful of dressed arugula. Drizzle lightly with wildflower honey. Finish with a few flakes of sea salt. Close with the top bun — optionally spread with a thin layer of ricotta as well — and serve immediately.
